articles.title: Apple is going to allow third-party app stores in Brazil, too
articles.summary: Apple is set to allow third-party app stores and for developers to use external payment systems on iOS in Brazil next year.
articles.body: Apple is set to allow third-party app stores on iOS in Brazil next year after settling with the country’s competition watchdog in a legal battle dating back to 2022, as reported by 9to5Mac. According to a machine translation of a press release from the Brazilian regulator CADE, it has approved a Term of Commitment to Termination (TCC) made by Apple that obligates the company to allow third-party app stores and let developers use external payment systems. Warnings about third-party app stores and external payment systems must also have neutral wording. Apple will be able to still charge fees, and the Brazilian publication Tecnoblog says in a machine translation that, according to CADE, those fees are: > Purchases within the App Store: > Commission of 25% (general) or 10% (special programs) > 5% fee if you use Apple’s payment system > App purchases on the App Store, but directed outside the store: > No fee if the routing involves static text (no clickable link/button) > 15% fee if the owner of the app puts a button/link and directs to payment on his own website (outside the app environment) > Alternative stores: > 5% of Core Technology Commission Apple has argued against opening up iOS on the grounds that it could compromise the platform’s security. But regulation in other countries has already forced the company to let users in Europe and Japan install third-party app stores, and in the US, Apple allows for external payment links. Apple has 105 days to put the changes into place, and if it doesn’t comply with its obligations, it could be subject to a fine of up to R$150 million (about $27 million). The company shared the following statement with 9to5Mac about the decision: > In order to comply with regulatory demands from CADE, Apple is making changes that will impact iOS apps in Brazil. While these changes will open new privacy and security risks to users, we have worked to maintain protections against some threats, including keeping in place important safeguards for younger users. These safeguards will not eliminate every risk, but they will help ensure that iOS remains the best, most secure mobile platform available in Brazil and we will continue to advocate on behalf of users and developers. Update, December 23rd: Added fee structure reported by Tecnoblog.

articles.title: Apple ordered to allow third-party app stores in Australia from 2027
articles.summary: Apple has been asked to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads and alternative payment services for users in Australia from March 1, 2027,
articles.body: Apple has been asked to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads and alternative payment services for users in Australia from March 1, 2027, following a Federal Court ruling. The court's orders follow its August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by limiting how users could download apps and make payments. The rules will apply to users whose Apple Account region is set to Australia, while developers enrolled in the Apple Developer Program worldwide can take part.Under the ruling, Apple must allow users to find, download, install and update apps through rival marketplaces and websites. It cannot charge users for accessing these options or create unnecessary barriers to their use.Developers must also receive the tools needed to distribute apps outside Apple's App Store on substantially the same terms as those for App Store distribution. Apple cannot penalise developers for using competing app stores or payment services.The ruling will also allow developers to offer alternative payment methods and link users to other ways to pay, including within apps distributed through the App Store. Apple cannot force developers to offer its own payment system alongside alternatives or require them to report or allow audits of transactions made through other services.Developers will also be able to offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple blocking them.The court has placed limits on the fees Apple can charge. Apple cannot collect fees on purchases made through alternative payment services or on websites linked from apps distributed outside the App Store. For apps distributed through its own store, fees will be capped at the rate charged for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine and reasonable additional costs linked to digital purchases.Apple also cannot require developers to use its payment system for content bought elsewhere as a condition for allowing alternative app distribution.However, security checks will remain in place. Apps downloaded outside the App Store must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and receive notarisation from Apple or a qualified third party. Apple cannot introduce disproportionate installation barriers, and any additional security requirements for competing payment services must be necessary and proportionate.Apple will be allowed to remove or disable apps installed from outside the App Store only in specific cases, such as harmful content, genuine security risks or legal requirements. It will not have to distribute rival app stores through its own store, but it cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones.Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and App Store security.The changes will take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply to the court between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for an extension until May 3, 2027.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Can a customer buy more than two iPhones at one time: Here’s what Apple Store 'warning' in India says
articles.summary: Apple has launched iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo.
articles.body: Apple has launched iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo. If you are planning to order multiple iPhones for your family or hand them out as gifts this festive season, there is an important checkout barrier to keep in mind. Apple has capped iPhone purchases at a strict two units per customer on its official online store. The purchase ceiling applies across Apple’s entire active iPhone catalog – a shopper can buy two units of an identical model or mix and match two completely different devices in a single cart. The system blocks users from adding a third unit, halting the checkout process immediately.When The Times of India Tech tried to purchase three iPhone 18 Pro models, the online store flashed a message saying, “A maximum of 2 iPhone can be purchased per customer. Please adjust the total quantity of iPhone in your order before checking out.” Notably, sources told TOI Tech that this limitation is not applicable on brick-and-mortar stores.Crucially, this is neither a temporary pilot nor a policy rolled out solely for new releases like the iPhone 18 Pro series or the foldable iPhone Duo. The rule has been actively enforced on Apple's online platform for some time and governs every iPhone model currently listed for sale.How the two-unit cart limit worksThe purchase cap does not simply limit shoppers from buying multiples of a specific variant, it restricts the total number of iPhones sitting in the digital shopping bag. In everyday practice, this means:A buyer can purchase two units of the exact same iPhone model.A buyer can select two entirely different iPhone models within the same transaction.As soon as an attempt is made to add a third handset – regardless of whether it is a different model, storage tier, or colour – Apple’s checkout system stops the order and serves an explicit warning prompt.Apple has not issued an official statement for this but this may be a mechanism to prevent gray-market resellers and scalpers from cornering stock through bulk acquisitions.You use AI every day. articles.title: The next iPhone Duo could have Face ID.
articles.summary:
That’s according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who said Apple is working on next-gen Duo protoypes that have the Face ID sensor located beneath the display on the outer screen. Being demoted to Touch ID has been a step back for the iPhone Duo, but in our review we said it’s “mostly painless” once you get used to it.

articles.title: The world’s first triple 200-megapixel camera phone is great
articles.summary: Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max benefits more from sensor size, dynamic range, and excellent software than sheer resolution.
articles.body: Oppo’s Find X10 Pro Max is the first phone with a triple 200-megapixel camera, which you’re likely to see as either a masterful feat of engineering or a load of hyped-up marketing nonsense. The truth is somewhere in the middle. We’ve seen 200-megapixel cameras in phones before, starting with 2022’s Moto X30 Pro. This year’s Vivo X300 Ultra was the first phone to feature two of them — with 200-megapixel main and telephoto cameras — and is still my favorite camera phone on the market. With the Find X10 Pro Max, Oppo is trying to do one better: It’s the first to use a 200-megapixel ultrawide camera too. Only the selfie camera runs at a more modest 50 megapixels. The Find X10 Pro Max’s cameras are excellent, lagging only a little behind the company’s top-tier Find X9 Ultra from earlier this year (in Oppo’s product lineup, as with rivals Xiaomi and Vivo, Pro Max phones still sit just below its top Ultra models). That’s only partly thanks to the megapixel count. The point of all those megapixels isn’t really to take 200-megapixel photos (though you can if you see fit — more on that later). Instead, like just about every phone camera from the last few years, Oppo is taking advantage of pixel-binning, which combines multiple nearby pixels into one. This gets you the best of both worlds: extra detail captured by the small, individual pixels and superior light capture from merging them together. One of the interesting changes Oppo has made is to actually reduce how much binning it uses. While most Android phones capture photos at 12 or 12.5 megapixels, regardless of their sensor resolution, the Find X10 Pro Max defaults to 26 megapixels across all three rear lenses, from 0.5x up to 9.9x zoom. That’s a similar resolution to Apple’s top iPhones, which now default to 24-megapixel shots across their 48-megapixel sensors, but still unusual for Android. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: By default, it means that shots from this phone are more detailed than on other Android rivals, and better suited to printing or cropping into. File sizes end up a little larger, of course: The Find X10 Pro Max’s 26-megapixel photos are typically 8 to 12MB, while 12.6-megapixel shots are closer to 4 to 6MB, though there’s a lot of variation. Binning to 26 megapixels rather than 12.6 has an obvious disadvantage beyond storage concerns, though: Less binning means worse light capture. In most light conditions that isn’t an issue, though, and the phone is smart enough to adapt when it becomes one, automatically dropping to 12.6 megapixels in darker scenes, sacrificing a little detail in order to maximize light when it’s in short supply. If you need high-resolution shots — or just want to force the matter and override the phone’s automatic adjustments — a high-resolution mode lets you shoot in either 50 megapixels or the full 200. Here file size balloons further, with 45 to 60MB files at the max resolution, but the 16,384 x 12,288 files are large and detailed enough to print at some size. To my surprise, I haven’t even seen much of a drop in low-light performance or dynamic range from shooting in this mode, though some difference will be inevitable in the darkest conditions. [Image: [Image: The thing with camera sensors, especially in a phone, is that resolution is only one factor — and not the most important. Sheer size matters more, which is why Oppo’s Find X9 Ultra still has an edge. The Find X10 Pro Max’s main camera uses a 1/1.3-inch-type sensor and an aperture of f/1.5, while its 3x telephoto is a little smaller at 1/1.56 inch, with a slower f/2.1 aperture. Both equivalents on the older Ultra phone use larger sensors capable of capturing more light even before pixel-binning kicks in. Only the ultrawide is improved here, with both a higher resolution and a bigger 1/1.56-inch sensor than the Ultra. But those upgrades to the ultrawide are crucial, because they help make this rear camera feel like a complete package. There’s no drop-off in resolution across the rear lenses, and only small shifts in sensor size and aperture. That means quality is consistent across the cameras, though the colors still vary a little, something I’d hope to see fine-tuned over time. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Part of the difference likely comes down to one feature you’ll only find on the main camera: what Oppo calls “DeepPix” dynamic range. It’s similar technology to LOFIC, seen on the likes of Xiaomi’s 17 Ultra and the recent Vivo X500 Pro Max, expanding dynamic range by capturing more information from highlights. Here, it enables a 17-stop dynamic range on the main camera, keeping light sources bright and punchy in nighttime scenes without blowing them out entirely. Only a handful of phones can match this, and none that you can buy in the US. [Image: [Image: [Image: That’s just the hardware. Photos are once again boosted by tuning from Hasselblad, with some of the techniques applied in the dramatic, filmic Hasselblad Master Mode now pulled into the main camera too, primarily less-saturated colors and deeper shadows. The Master Mode still pushes the effect further if you prefer. Eighteen built-in film simulations allow more varied color profiles, and each can be tweaked further with a simple grid that adjusts tone and saturation. [Image: Each film look can be adjusted using the grid and slider at the bottom. Video has its own tricks. All three rear lenses can record at up to 120fps in 4K or 30fps in 8K, and a Pro Video mode lets you apply LUTs, record with Oppo’s O-Log2 for more post-production options, and even shoot in open gate, taking full advantage of the full sensor. Oppo’s high-end hardware accessories are back too. A teleconverter lens can be mounted on top of the telephoto lens for improved long-range photography, while a video accessory kit from Tilta includes cooling, a light, a substantial camera grip, tripod mount, polarizing filter, and more. I haven’t even spoken about the rest of the phone: a big 7,150mAh battery (even bigger outside of Europe at 8,000mAh) that lasts two days easy; a MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset that hasn’t stuttered once; a 144Hz, 1.5K OLED display with 3,600 nits of peak brightness. Perhaps just as importantly, a design that fits all those camera specs into a relatively modest camera island, instead of the colossal ring of lenses that’s become typical on Chinese Ultra phones. [Image: The Find X10 Pro Max is launching across Europe and elsewhere, but not the US. In a flagship phone like this, none of that matters as much as the cameras. Meanwhile, Oppo’s marketing team would have you believe that in a camera like this, nothing matters as much as the megapixels. That’s not entirely true. The Find X10 Pro Max’s camera is really as good as it is because all three lenses use fairly large sensors; because the impressive Hasselblad color science has been further refined in the default camera mode; because the main lens has an almost unprecedented dynamic range for a phone. The extra megapixels are the cherry on top. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge
